title: Not Everything Is a Table

post.author: u/lamplit_inventory_delphine
post.title: I do the night inventory at a curiosity shop. Every night a query works out who owned each object, and on Tuesday it ran until dawn and said we have owned the same music box three times.

blocks.text: Rookwood's is a curiosity shop on Wickery Row: ship's clocks, glass eyes, a heron under a dome, drawers of keys that fit nothing. I do the inventory at night. Mrs Rookwood took the shop over from her uncle in 2006, and for two winters she has typed his card ledger, eleven drawers of index cards, into the computer. It went into PostgreSQL, a widely used database program, as one table, a grid of rows and columns like a spreadsheet. She calls it the ledger. On Monday she typed in the last drawer.

Every kind of fact went in as a row, one line of the grid: objects, people, sales, repairs, even the baskets, the half-finished orders, from our little website. The table has 61 columns, one for every kind of fact anyone ever wrote on a card, and on most rows 53 of them are empty. It holds 40,000 rows: 6,140 objects, 25,180 sales and 8,680 everything else. Beside it is a readings table. Each of our 14 glass cabinets has a humidity sensor, a small gauge of damp in the air, that writes a reading a minute, 22,075,200 rows in three years, and the morning humidity chart takes 44.2 seconds to draw.

At 23:00 every night a query, a question written for the database, works out each object's chain of owners: who sold it to whom, and who those people sold it on to. Half the old cards have no date, so the chain follows names: the buyer on one sale is the seller on the next. Mrs Rookwood wrote the query from a book. It joins the ledger to itself six times. A join matches rows with other rows, here ledger rows with ledger rows: a self-join for each step. Each step goes like this: take the last buyer's name, search the ledger for a sale where that name is the seller, and add that sale to the chain. It has finished a little later every week. On Tuesday it ran until dawn. In the log below, the first two lines show when the job started and finished. Each later line shows the lot number, the object and the owners in the chain it found, and the last line is the job's note:

Tue 23:00:00  owner chains  started: 6,140 objects, 6 steps each
Wed 05:49:20  owner chains  finished after 6 h 49 min 20 s
   ...
   lot 0417  music box  Marchetti, shop, Pendle, shop, Pendarves
   lot 0417  music box  Marchetti, shop, Pendle, shop, Pendle, shop, Pendle
             the shop has owned this object 3 times

The line above the last is the box's story as the cards tell it. Marchetti sold it to us in 1962, we sold it to a Pendle in 1974, Pendle sold it back in 1991, and we sold it again in 2003, to a Pendarves. Then the last line goes back to the shop, and back again.
Mrs Rookwood has never seen a music box in this shop. By the ledger, we have owned it three times.
She wants the chains printed on every label before the spring fair. A dealer there told her the trouble is the table: "Nobody keeps this kind of thing in tables any more." What should she change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Before anyone moves a single row, write down what the shop asks of its data, and how often. Each of those is an access pattern: fetch one object by its lot number, follow a chain of owners step by step, read each cabinet's readings over a stretch of time, get and set a basket. Every kind of database is built for some patterns and charges you for others. Then read Tuesday's numbers. How many rows does one step of one chain read? Is there an index, a sorted list like the one at the back of a book, helping the database find the next sale? Then follow the music box's cards by hand, buyer to seller, as the query does. A cycle is a chain that comes back to a sale it has already used. Does this one, and what in the query would ever stop it? PostgreSQL can also follow a chain with a recursive query. It works in steps: find the first sale, use its buyer to find the next sale, feed that result back in, and repeat until a step finds nothing new. What would that do here, as the cards stand? Last, the chart: 44.2 seconds to draw a year it drew yesterday. How much of that year changed overnight?

replies.author: u/lamplit_inventory_delphine
replies.text: I followed them by hand. From the 1991 card the shop is the seller again, and there are two cards where we sold the box: 1974 and 2003. Without dates, nothing tells the query which one comes next. And the only index on the ledger is on the lot number. The 1991 card was in Monday's drawer.

comments.author: u/one_drawer_eulalia
comments.text: The 61 columns are the tell. A document database stores each record as a document, like a filled-in form: a bundle of labelled fields, written in a text format called JSON, read and written whole. The documents in one collection, its word for a group, don't need the same fields: a clock has a maker and a movement, a heron has a taxidermist. MongoDB, a popular document database, uses a shop's product catalogue as the example in its own guides. No more empty columns, and no schema, the fixed list of columns every row must fit, to fight every time someone writes a new kind of fact on a card. We moved our auction house's catalogue into one last year and never looked back. Documents fit everything a shop like yours keeps.

comments.author: u/all_threads_tiberius
comments.text: Documents still can't follow a chain. Everything in that ledger is a relationship: a person sold an object to a person, who sold it on. A graph database stores exactly that, like a map of dots and strings. Each object and person is a dot, called a node, and the relationships between them are kept right beside them. Following a chain is a walk: start at a node, follow one string to the next node, and repeat. No joins at all, no matching of rows between tables. Owner chains, provenance, who knew whom: that's what graphs are for, and it's where every serious dataset is heading. Put the whole shop in one and the chain query is three lines.

replies.author: u/lamplit_inventory_delphine
replies.text: Mrs Rookwood's nephew says he could move everything over a few weekends.

comments.author: u/greenhouse_probe_clarimond
comments.text: Your sensors are the easy part. Readings like yours are time-series data: values stamped with the time, written in time order and read back by time range. A time-series database is built for them. It keeps rollups, summaries worked out ahead of time. Every hour a job reads that hour's readings for each cabinet, works out one average, and saves it, so a chart reads a few rows instead of every reading. And a retention rule deletes raw readings once they're older than a set age. Our greenhouse runs one for its probes. Beside it is a key-value store, which keeps one value under one name, like a cloakroom ticket, for the till's baskets. And a document store holds the plant records. Use the right tool for each job.

reply.prompt: The spring fair is five weeks away. Mrs Rookwood wants a chain of owners on every label, and the chart quick in the mornings. What should she change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Move everything into a document database: every object keeps only the fields it needs, and there's no 61-column table left to fight with.
options.verdict: Fits the objects, not the jobs
options.part2: Mrs Rookwood's nephew spent three weekends moving the shop into a document store: one document for each object, each person and each sale, every one with its own fields. Item lookups stayed at a millisecond, a thousandth of a second. The chains no longer run all night. The app follows each chain itself: fetch a sale, read its buyer, fetch the next sale, and stop at a sale already on its path. All 6,140 chains take 31.3 seconds. But nothing in the move helped the chart. It now reads the year's 7,358,400 readings from documents, 29.4 seconds every morning. And with no schema, the new sensor in cabinet 9 writes its reading under hum, not humidity. Nothing refused it, and cabinet 9's line on the chart has been empty for a fortnight.
options.senior: A document database fits records whose fields vary and that are read whole, and the shop's objects are exactly that. But moving everything doesn't change the access patterns. The chains still follow one sale to the next, now one round trip a step in the app: a question sent to the database and an answer back. The readings still need range reads and rollups the move didn't bring. The database stops checking the shape of each write, so your code has to. And Tuesday's slow job was a missing index and a loop with nothing to stop it, both fixable where the data already was.

options.text: Move everything into a graph database: objects, people and sales become nodes and links, and owner chains are exactly what graphs do.
options.part2: The nephew moved the shop into a graph store over a month: objects, people and sales as nodes, each sale linked to its seller, its buyer and its object. The chains are a joy. Written so that no path uses a sale twice, all 6,140 take 0.31 seconds, and the music box's ends with Pendarves. Then the readings: 22,075,200 of them, one node each, and the 12-month chart now takes 2 minutes 27 seconds every morning. Item lookups went from 1 ms to 2 ms, thousandths of a second, which nobody noticed. Mrs Rookwood noticed the chart.
options.senior: A graph store makes walking relationships many steps deep cheap, because each node keeps its links beside it. That fits the owner chains and nothing else in the shop. Readings are ranges by time, items are lookups by key, baskets are get and set, and a graph store is built for none of them. Moving everything to serve one nightly job makes the other workloads, the other kinds of work, worse. A recursive query with an index serves that job in seconds.

options.text: Keep PostgreSQL: a recursive query that stops at cycles, an index on sales, hourly rollups for readings. Add stores only when needed.
options.part2: Mrs Rookwood moved the 25,180 sales into their own narrow table, sales(object_id, seller, buyer, sold_on): just four columns, the object, the seller, the buyer and the date. She added an index on (object_id, seller), so the database jumps straight to the next sale. She rewrote the job as a recursive query with PostgreSQL's CYCLE clause on the sale id, which keeps each chain's path and stops at any sale already on it. On the first night it finished at 23:00:03, after 3.1 seconds. The music box now reads Marchetti, shop, Pendle, shop, Pendarves: we owned it twice, 1962 to 1974 and 1991 to 2003, and the branch that went back to the 1974 sale stopped, marked as a cycle. Thirty-seven chains longer than six sales printed whole for the first time. The readings went into a table partitioned by month, split into one piece per month, with an hourly rollup table filled by a job every hour. Once three years of rollups were in, a retention rule began deleting raw readings older than 30 days, leaving 604,800. The chart takes 0.25 seconds. It's still one database to run and back up, and a graph store stays on the list for the day the chains crawl again.
options.senior: Start from the access patterns, not the store. The all-night run was a missing index and a chain that could go round in circles, and PostgreSQL fixes both in place: a recursive query that never reuses a sale on one path, and an index for each step. The readings are time-series data, and a table split by time, with hourly rollups and a retention rule, serves them inside the database you already back up. A relational database, one built on tables like PostgreSQL, stays the system of record for most products: the one copy that counts. Add another store when a pattern proves it needs one, and count what it costs to run, secure and keep in step.

options.text: Give each kind of data its own store now: key-value for baskets, documents for objects, a graph for chains, time-series for readings.
options.verdict: Trade-off: fast, and four to run
options.part2: The nephew set up four: a key-value store for baskets, a document store for objects and people, a graph store for the chains and a time-series store for the readings. Every workload is quick: chains 0.31 seconds, the chart 0.25, a basket 0.5 ms. The sales live in the document store and are copied to the graph store for the chains: two writes, and no single transaction, the all-or-nothing wrapper that makes both happen or neither. On the Saturday of the fair the copy failed for an hour, and three labels printed that afternoon left out a sale made that morning. A basket held a clock sold at the till ten minutes earlier, and nothing in the basket store could know. Mrs Rookwood now runs four databases, each to back up, patch (install fixes on) and secure, and she is one person.
options.senior: Each store fits its workload, and the times show it. The price is everything between them: four things to run, back up, patch and secure, and data that lives in two of them with no transaction across both, so the copies drift. That trade makes sense when one database truly can't serve a pattern, at a scale where the gain pays for the people. Here PostgreSQL serves all four in seconds or less, so the extra stores buy speed nobody needed.

sim.title: Choose a store for each job at Rookwood's
sim.lede: You're Mrs Rookwood, replaying Tuesday night from 23:00 at an hour a second. The shop has four workloads, and you pick the store each one runs on: item lookups (one object by lot number), the owner chains for all 6,140 objects, the cabinet sensors (14 writes a minute, and a chart of each cabinet's last 12 months) and the website's baskets. The stores are PostgreSQL, key-value, document, wide-column (rows grouped into partitions by a partition key and sorted by time inside each, like Discord's messages), graph and time-series. Pick how the chain is followed: six self-joins, as now; a recursive query with no cycle guard; or one with a cycle guard, a rule that stops a chain at a sale already on its path. For PostgreSQL you can index the sales on (object, seller), and give the readings a time-partitioned table with hourly rollups and raw readings kept 30 days. Times come from a simple cost model: with no index every chain step reads all 40,000 ledger rows at 60,000 a second, an indexed step takes 0.1 ms, and readings are read at 500,000 a second; the other stores' costs are in the terms. A job still running at 07:00 is stopped. Changing anything replays the night, and the four option buttons load the four replies. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: let the night run as built. The job finishes at 05:49:20, after 6 h 49 min 20 s, and prints the music box with the shop as owner 3 times. Add the sales index: 3.7 s, but still 3 times, with 37 chains cut at 6 steps. Switch to a recursive query with no cycle guard: it never ends, index or not. Choose one that stops at cycles and turn the index off: 5 h 48 min. Turn the index back on: 3.1 s, and the box ends with Pendarves. Turn on hourly rollups: the chart falls from 44.2 s to 0.25 s. Put the readings on a key-value store and see what happens to the chart. Then press the four option buttons and compare the times, the stores to run and the data kept in two stores.

explain.oneLine: The shop never owned the box a third time. The query followed names, not dates, so from the 1991 buyback it found the 1974 sale again and went round; and with no index on the sales, each of its 36,840 steps read the whole ledger.

steps.title: Tuesday: no index, and a chain that can go round.
steps.text: The job joins the ledger to itself six times, one self-join per step, for each of the 6,140 objects: 36,840 steps. Each step has to find the sale whose seller is the last buyer. An index, a sorted list pointing to rows, would let it jump straight there. But the only index is on the lot number, so each step reads all 40,000 rows, top to bottom, and keeps the ones that match. That's 1,473,600,000 rows a night. The shop's server, the computer the database runs on, reads 60,000 of these wide rows a second, so it takes 6 hours 49 minutes 20 seconds. The cost grows with the objects times the rows, so every drawer Mrs Rookwood typed in made the job later. Monday's drawer also held the 1991 card, where Pendle sold the box back. Half the cards have no date, so the query matches buyer to seller by name alone. From the 1991 sale the shop is the seller again, and two sales match: 2003, the true next step, and 1974, which leads back to 1991. That's a cycle. Six joins stopped the walk after six sales, so it printed the shop three times instead of looping forever. The same six-join limit also cut short the 37 objects with more than six sales.

steps.title: Five families, five access patterns.
steps.text: A relational database keeps data in tables of rows and columns, and you ask it questions in SQL, the standard language for tables. NoSQL is a loose name for databases that don't work that way. Each family is built around one access pattern and charges for others. Key-value: get and set one value by its key, its name, like a basket or a session (one visitor's visit), very fast. It has no joins and usually no range reads, which fetch everything between two values. Document: one record whose fields vary, read and written whole, like objects with different details. MongoDB's docs say data that's accessed together should be stored together. The price is that links between documents are followed by your code. Wide-column: huge data that is mostly added to, never changed, grouped by a partition key and sorted inside each group. The partition key is the value that decides which group, and so which machine, a row lives in. It's read one group at a time, in time order, like Discord's messages per channel; Discord is a chat app. The price is that you design tables for your queries, and a query the key doesn't fit is slow or impossible. Graph: nodes and relationships, stored side by side, so following relationships many steps deep is cheap, like owner chains. Ranges and reading everything in bulk are not its job. Time-series: readings stamped with the time, written in order, read by time range, rolled up and expired, like the cabinet sensors. It doesn't look things up by key or by seller.

steps.title: What PostgreSQL already does.
steps.text: A relational database does much of this well enough. A recursive query, written WITH RECURSIVE, runs in steps. First a starting part finds each object's first sale. Then a repeating part takes the rows the last step found and looks up the next sale for each. Those new rows are fed back in, and the repeating part runs again. It stops when a step returns nothing new. PostgreSQL's docs warn that the recursive part must eventually return no tuples, its word for rows, or else the query will loop indefinitely. That is what a cycle does to it. The CYCLE clause adds a guard, in three steps. It watches a column, here the sale id. It keeps the path, the list of sale ids so far. When a row reaches a sale already on its path, it marks that row as a cycle and stops following it. With the sales in a narrow table indexed on (object_id, seller), each step is one index lookup: 31,320 lookups, 3.1 seconds. In the sim the index alone, with six joins, takes 3.7 seconds and still prints the shop three times, and the cycle guard alone takes 5 hours 48 minutes: the job needs both. For readings, three changes work together. Split the table by time, one piece per month. Every hour, a job reads the last hour's readings for each cabinet, works out the average, and writes one row to a rollup table. Then a retention job deletes raw rows older than 30 days, but only once they are rolled up; delete first and that detail is gone for good. Together they take the 12-month chart from 22,075,200 rows to 122,640, and from 44.2 seconds to 0.25. TimescaleDB, an add-on for PostgreSQL, builds in the same ideas as hypertables and continuous aggregates.

steps.title: When to add a store, and what it costs.
steps.text: Add a store when an access pattern proves, with numbers, that the database you have can't serve it. Discord moved its messages off MongoDB once the data and the index no longer fit in RAM, the server's fast working memory. Then count the cost. Each store is one more thing to run, patch, back up, watch and secure, and someone has to know it at 3 AM. Keeping data in two stores usually works like this. The app writes to the first store. Then it, or a job, writes the same change to the second. A transaction, the all-or-nothing wrapper, can't cover both. So if the second write fails, arrives late, or a delete reaches only one store, the two disagree. Keep one store as the system of record, the one whose copy counts, and treat the others as copies you can rebuild. In the sim, putting each workload on its own store makes everything fast and leaves four stores to run, with the sales and people kept in two.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the night after. The owner-chain job is a recursive query that stops at cycles and finishes in 3.1 seconds, with the shop owning the music box twice. It does one index lookup a step on the sales table, which holds object, seller, buyer and date and is indexed on object and seller. A graph store, greyed out, sits below the sales table: a copy only if the chains ever crawl again. On the right, the morning chart reads the hourly rollups, one row per cabinet-hour, 122,640 for 12 months, in 0.25 seconds. The readings table is partitioned by time and keeps 30 days of raw readings, 604,800 rows, rolled up every hour.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the night after, all in PostgreSQL. The sales have their own narrow table, indexed on object and seller, and the job is a recursive query that stops at any sale already on its path: 3.1 seconds, and the shop owns the music box twice. A graph store is drawn greyed out, as a copy to add only if the chains ever crawl again. The readings go into a table partitioned by time that keeps 30 days of raw readings, rolled up every hour, and the morning chart reads 122,640 hourly rows in 0.25 seconds.

fix.title: The fix: index the steps, stop at cycles, roll up the readings, keep one database
fix.text: Move the 25,180 sales out of the ledger into a narrow table, sales(object_id, seller, buyer, sold_on), with an index on (object_id, seller), so each step of a chain is one index lookup. Rewrite the job as a recursive query, WITH RECURSIVE, with a CYCLE clause on the sale id, so a path never uses a sale twice. Where a card has a date, also require each next sale to be later. Check the plan, the database's own account of how it will run the query, with EXPLAIN ANALYZE: 3.1 seconds, not 6 hours 49 minutes. Move the readings into a table partitioned by month, add an hourly rollup table filled by a job each hour, and once the rollups cover the old data, delete raw readings older than 30 days. Point the chart at the rollups: 0.25 seconds. Keep PostgreSQL as the system of record, and write down the number that would justify a graph store: if the chains ever take longer than the night, measure again.

limits: A cycle guard stops the walk. It doesn't decide which branch is true. Without dates, the box's 1991 sale still matches both 1974 and 2003, and the guard only refuses the one already on the path. The cards with dates should order the steps, and someone should date the rest, or the chain stays a best guess.

Rollups throw detail away. Once raw readings older than 30 days are deleted, nobody can ask what cabinet 4 did between 03:12 and 03:14 last spring, only its hourly average. Choose the rollups (average, minimum, maximum) and the raw window before deleting anything, because deletion can't be undone.

The 61-column ledger is still a modeling problem, which none of this fixes. PostgreSQL can hold the facts that vary from object to object in a jsonb column, one that holds a document-like bundle of fields, or in separate tables. Which to choose is a question about access patterns, and it's the next case's.

explain.seniorTake: Not everything is a table, and most things fit in one anyway. Start from the access patterns: what's asked, how often, how fast it must be, how much data. Then check whether the database you already run can serve each one with the right index, query or table shape. A relational database usually stays the system of record, the copy that counts, and does much of this well enough. Reach for another store when a pattern proves, with numbers, that it needs one: more writes a second than one machine can take, data that outgrows memory, walks too deep for any join. And count the bill before you add it: one more thing to run, back up, secure and keep in agreement with the first, forever. The tempting mistakes go both ways: moving everything to suit one workload, and giving every workload its own store.

realWorld.title: Discord, January 2017: from MongoDB to Cassandra
realWorld.text: Discord is a chat app. In How Discord Stores Billions of Messages, Stanislav Vishnevskiy describes starting with messages in "a MongoDB collection with a single compound index on channel_id and created_at." Around November 2015 Discord reached 100 million stored messages, and "the data and the index could no longer fit in RAM and latencies started to become unpredictable." RAM is the server's fast working memory, and latency is how long each answer takes. Before choosing, the team studied its patterns: "our reads were extremely random and our read/write ratio was about 50/50." It wrote down its requirements and concluded: "Cassandra was the only database that fulfilled all of our requirements." Cassandra is a widely used free wide-column database. The post describes it as a KKV store, a key then a second key: "The first K is the partition key and is used to determine which node the data lives on and where it is found on disk," and the second, the clustering key, "acts as both a primary key within the partition and how the rows are sorted." Since "all queries operate on a channel", channel_id became the partition key. To keep partitions small, Discord also grouped messages by time into buckets, about 10 days a bucket, and "our new primary key became ((channel_id, bucket), message_id)." It ran "a 12 node cluster with a replica factor of 3." That is 12 machines working as one, with three copies of every message.

realWorld.title: Discord, March 2023: trillions of messages, and ScyllaDB
realWorld.text: In How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages, Bo Ingram writes: "In 2017, we ran 12 Cassandra nodes, storing billions of messages. At the beginning of 2022, it had 177 nodes with trillions of messages." The model kept its shape: "We partition our messages by the channel they’re sent in, along with a bucket, which is a static time window." Discord switched the messages database to ScyllaDB, a database that works like Cassandra, in May 2022, "going from running 177 Cassandra nodes to just 72 ScyllaDB nodes." Fetching historical messages "had a p99 of between 40-125ms on Cassandra, with ScyllaDB having a nice and chill 15ms p99 latency", and inserts went from 5-70ms p99 to a steady 5ms p99. The p99 is the wait that 99 of every 100 requests stay within, and ms means thousandths of a second. The access pattern, messages per channel read by time, stayed the same through both moves.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL: recursive queries and cycle detection
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL 18's page on WITH queries says the RECURSIVE modifier "changes WITH from a mere syntactic convenience into a feature that accomplishes things not otherwise possible in standard SQL. Using RECURSIVE, a WITH query can refer to its own output." It notes that "Recursive queries are typically used to deal with hierarchical or tree-structured data." On cycles it warns: "When working with recursive queries it is important to be sure that the recursive part of the query will eventually return no tuples, or else the query will loop indefinitely." UNION and UNION ALL are the two ways to stack each step's rows onto the last. UNION, instead of UNION ALL, can help by throwing away rows that repeat exactly. But a query that also outputs a depth, how many steps in it is, never repeats a row exactly, so it needs a path. The built-in form: "The CYCLE clause specifies first the list of columns to track for cycle detection, then a column name that will show whether a cycle has been detected, and finally the name of another column that will track the path."

realWorld.title: MongoDB: documents, and data accessed together
realWorld.text: MongoDB's data modeling page says it "has a flexible data model that allows you to store polymorphic data", meaning "Documents within a single collection are not required to have the same set of fields." Its core principle: "data that's accessed together should be stored together. You should structure your data model based on your application's data access patterns to optimize performance." One of its examples is a clothing store's product catalog: "Different products have different attributes and might have different document fields and field types. Despite these differences, you can store all of the products in the same collection." It models relationships by embedding or referencing.

realWorld.title: Neo4j: nodes, relationships and no JOINs
realWorld.text: Neo4j's introduction says a Neo4j graph database "stores data as nodes, relationships, and properties instead of in tables or documents." Properties are details stored on a node or relationship. It argues that "relational databases use computing-wise expensive JOIN operations or cross-looks", and that "Graph databases do not use JOINs. Rather, relationships are stored natively alongside the data elements (nodes)".

realWorld.title: Neo4j: relationships and traversals
realWorld.text: Neo4j's concepts page says "Neo4j uses a property graph database model", that relationships "describe a connection between a source node and a target node" and always have a direction and a type, and that "Traversing a graph means visiting nodes by following relationships according to some rules." These are the claims of a company that sells a graph database; for a few thousand chains a night, an indexed recursive query served the shop in seconds.

realWorld.title: TimescaleDB: hypertables
realWorld.text: TimescaleDB is an add-on for PostgreSQL. Its docs, now on Tiger Data's site, describe hypertables as "PostgreSQL tables that automatically partition your time-series data by time and optionally by other dimensions", split into chunks "that hold data from a specific time range. For example, one day or one week."

realWorld.title: TimescaleDB: continuous aggregates
realWorld.text: TimescaleDB does rollups with continuous aggregates: "Continuous aggregates in TimescaleDB are a kind of hypertable that is refreshed automatically in the background as new data is added, or old data is modified." The docs compare them with PostgreSQL's own materialized views, a query's answer saved like a table and rebuilt when asked: continuous aggregates "have a much lower maintenance burden than regular PostgreSQL materialized views, because the whole view is not created from scratch on each refresh." It's the same idea as the shop's rollup table, kept inside PostgreSQL.

realWorld.title: Prometheus: everything is a time series
realWorld.text: Prometheus is a free monitoring system, a program that collects measurements about other systems. Its data model page says it "fundamentally stores all data as time series: streams of timestamped values belonging to the same metric and the same set of labeled dimensions." A metric is one thing being measured. Each series is identified by its metric name and labels, name-and-value pairs such as the HTTP method, the kind of web request. Uptime checks, tests of whether a site answers, like the ones Nightwatch stores, are this kind of data.

realWorld.title: Prometheus: kept for a while
realWorld.text: Prometheus keeps data for a set time. Its storage page says --storage.tsdb.retention.time sets how long to retain samples, and "If neither this flag nor storage.tsdb.retention.size is set, the retention time defaults to 15d." 15d means 15 days.

asked: SQL or NoSQL for this design?
Which database would you use for chat messages, for a social graph, and for metrics?
When would you add a second datastore?
interview.answer: Don't answer with a brand; answer with access patterns. List what the system asks of its data, how often, how fast, and how much data there is. Start from a relational database as the system of record, the copy that counts. It serves many shapes of question over shared data, with joins, transactions and constraints, rules every row must obey. Check what the right index, query or table shape does before reaching further. A recursive query with a cycle guard walks a hierarchy, a family-tree shape. A table split by time, with rollups and a retention rule, serves metrics, measurements over time, at moderate scale. Then match patterns to families. Chat messages: huge, mostly added and never changed, read per channel by time. So a wide-column store partitioned by channel and a time bucket, as Discord did on Cassandra and later ScyllaDB, or a sharded relational table, split over machines, while the scale allows. A social graph: friends of friends many steps deep is a graph store's pattern, though two steps with good indexes is often fine in SQL. Metrics: a time-series store, with rollups and retention, such as Prometheus or TimescaleDB. Add a second datastore when a pattern proves, with numbers, that the first can't serve it, and say what it costs: another system to run, back up and secure, and data written to two places with no single transaction, so one store stays the system of record and the other is a copy you can rebuild.

terms.def: A shop that sells odd old things: clocks, glass eyes, keys, stuffed birds. Rookwood's, on Wickery Row, is this case's.
Mrs Rookwood's uncle's records: eleven drawers of index cards, one card per object, sale or person, many without dates.
The one PostgreSQL table Mrs Rookwood typed the cards into: 61 columns, one per kind of fact, and 40,000 rows, most of their cells empty.
The number a shop gives each object it sells. The music box is lot 0417, and the ledger's only index is on lot numbers.
The list of things a website visitor means to buy, kept under a basket id until they pay or leave.
A small device that measures how much water vapour is in the air. Each of the 14 glass cabinets has one, writing a reading a minute.
The PostgreSQL table the cabinet sensors write to: 20,160 readings a day, 22,075,200 rows in three years, no index, nothing deleted.
Everyone who owned an object, in order: who sold it to whom, then who they sold it on to. The shop's nightly job works one out for each object.
The history of who has owned an object. Dealers print it on labels because it helps show an object is what it claims to be.
Matching a table's rows with other rows of the same table, such as a sale with the next sale of the same object. Like laying two copies of one list side by side.
One kind of question an app asks of its data, and how often: fetch one record by key, follow links many steps, read a time range.
A database that keeps data in tables of rows and columns, like linked spreadsheets, and answers questions written in SQL, the standard language for tables. PostgreSQL is one.
A loose name for databases that aren't relational tables queried with SQL, such as key-value, document, wide-column, graph and time-series stores.
A store that keeps each record as a document, like a filled-in form: labelled fields, read and written whole. Documents in one group needn't share fields.
A group of documents in MongoDB, like a table, except its documents don't have to have the same fields.
MongoDB's phrase for records of one kind whose fields, or the types of their fields, differ from one record to the next.
Two ways a document database links data: put the related data inside the document, or store its id and fetch it separately.
A store that keeps data as nodes and the relationships between them, each node's relationships stored beside it, so following them is cheap.
In a graph database, a node is a thing, such as a person or an object; a relationship joins two nodes and has a type and a direction, such as SOLD_TO.
Neo4j's model: nodes with labels, relationships with a type and a direction, and properties, named details, on both.
Answering a question by walking a graph from node to node along relationships, following some rules.
A widely used graph database, built on the property graph model.
A store whose rows are grouped by a partition key and sorted inside each group, built for huge data that is mostly added to and read one group at a time. Cassandra is one.
The first part of a row's key in Cassandra. It decides which machines hold the row, and rows with the same partition key are stored together, like one drawer.
The second part of a row's key in Cassandra. It picks and sorts rows inside one partition, like the order of cards in a drawer, such as a message id that rises with time.
Discord's 2017 description of Cassandra: a first key that picks the partition, then a second that picks and sorts the row inside it.
A fixed window of time, about 10 days in 2017, added to the channel id in Discord's partition key so no partition grows forever.
A database that speaks Cassandra's query language and stores data the same wide-column way. Discord moved its messages to it in 2022.
Timestamped values written in time order, such as a sensor reading every minute, and read back by time range.
A store built for time-series data: fast appends, reads by time range, and built-in rollups and retention.
A summary worked out ahead of time, such as one average per cabinet per hour, so a chart reads a few rows instead of every reading.
A rule that deletes data once it is older than a set age, such as raw readings after 30 days, usually after they've been rolled up.
A PostgreSQL table split into partitions by time, such as one a month, so a query for a time range reads only those partitions and old ones drop in one go.
A SQL query that feeds its own results back into itself, step after step, until a step returns no new rows. PostgreSQL writes it WITH RECURSIVE.
A smaller, named query written first, after the word WITH, that the main query then uses. Also called a common table expression. WITH RECURSIVE lets it use its own results.
A chain that comes back to something it has already passed, such as the music box's 1991 sale leading back to the 1974 sale.
A rule that stops a chain when it reaches something already on its path. PostgreSQL's CYCLE clause adds one to a recursive query.
A PostgreSQL add-on to a recursive query. You name the columns to watch, a column that says a cycle was found, and a column that keeps the path walked so far.
SQL ways to stack two results. UNION drops rows that repeat exactly; UNION ALL keeps them.
PostgreSQL's word for a row.
A PostgreSQL column that holds a document-like bundle of labelled fields, so rows of one table can carry fields that differ from row to row.
A query's answer saved like a table, like a printed report, and refreshed when asked. PostgreSQL rebuilds the whole answer on each refresh.
An add-on that gives PostgreSQL time-series features, such as hypertables and continuous aggregates. Its docs now live on Tiger Data's site.
A TimescaleDB table split into chunks by time automatically, and queried like any PostgreSQL table.
One piece of a hypertable, holding the rows for one time range, such as a day or a week.
A TimescaleDB rollup that keeps itself up to date in the background as rows arrive or change, instead of being rebuilt from scratch, like a running total.
A free monitoring system that collects measurements about other systems. It stores each one as a time series and keeps them for 15 days unless told otherwise.
A name-and-value pair, such as the kind of web request, that tells apart time series measuring the same thing. Like a tag on a jar.
The share of time a site answered its checks, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days.
Any database the sim can put a workload on: PostgreSQL, key-value, document, wide-column, graph or time-series.
The sim's rule for time: an unindexed chain step reads all 40,000 ledger rows at 60,000 a second, an indexed step is 0.1 ms, and readings are read at 500,000 a second.
By key: key-value 0.5 ms, document 1, wide-column and graph 2. Chain step: key-value 0.5 ms, document 1, wide-column 2, graph 0.01. Readings a second: wide-column 1M, document 250k, graph 50k.
Sales and people stored both where items live and where chains run: two writes, no single transaction across them, so the copies can disagree.
Reading each change from a database's log, its running list of every change, and copying it to another store as it happens, so the copy trails by seconds, not a day.
A rule in ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard companies are checked against: delete information from systems and disks once it is no longer needed.

atWork: Picture a common setup. A team added a search store, a second database built for searching text, beside its PostgreSQL database for one feature, product search. The app copies products into it: two writes, with no single transaction, the all-or-nothing wrapper, across them. A year on, a renamed product still shows its old name in search, a deleted one can still be found and clicked, and once a quarter someone rebuilds the copy by hand. Look for the same in your own systems. List every datastore, every database or store, you run, and for each one the access patterns it actually serves, with how often and how fast. Mark which one is the system of record, the copy that counts, for each kind of data, and how every copy is kept in step: a nightly job, two writes from the app, or changes copied from the database's log as they happen. Ask what happens to a delete, and when the copy was last rebuilt from scratch. Then, for each extra store, ask whether the main database could now serve that pattern with an index, a recursive query or a better table, and what the store costs in running, backups, patching and security. Before adding the next one, write down the number that proves the need. This rehearses Nightwatch's N2 Build Night, which unlocks after this case and the next. Uptime checks, tests of whether a site answers, are time-series data. So store raw results in a table split by time. Add minute, hour and day rollups filled by a job, and a retention job that deletes old raw results. Write an uptime query over any window that reads the rollups. Record in docs/decisions.md why you rolled up and what you lose by doing it. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard, control A.8.10 (information deletion) asks that information be deleted when it is no longer required. A written retention rule, with a job that enforces it and its logs, is the kind of evidence an auditor looks for. Build it in from the first table rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's app keeps users, posts and follows, who follows whom, in PostgreSQL. A new feature shows the people your friends follow, two steps out, and the first rough version of the query takes 9 seconds. An engineer proposes moving the whole app into a graph database. What do you advise?

keyIdeas.idea: Look at the query first: EXPLAIN it, index the follows table, and if it goes deeper, use a recursive query that stops at cycles
Keep PostgreSQL as the system of record; don't move everything for one feature
Add a graph store only if measurements show the pattern still needs one, and count its cost: one more store to run, and copies to keep in step

recall.model: Don't move the app for one feature. First EXPLAIN the slow query, asking the database to show how it runs it. Two steps out is two joins on the follows table, and with an index on (follower_id, followed_id) that's usually milliseconds, not 9 seconds. If the feature later needs many steps, PostgreSQL can walk them with a recursive query that stops at cycles, because people follow each other back. Keep PostgreSQL as the system of record for users, posts and follows. Only if measurements show the walks are still too slow, add a graph store as a copy of the follows for that one feature, and count the cost first: another store to run, back up and secure, and two writes with no single transaction, so the copy needs keeping in step.

recall.prompt: Discord stores messages partitioned by channel and a time bucket, writes them all day long, and mostly reads one channel's recent messages. Which family is that access pattern built for?
options: Key-value: each message saved under its own id
Graph: messages linked to their channel and author
Wide-column: partitioned by key, sorted by time inside
Document: each channel as one document holding its messages
recall.why: Huge, append-heavy data read by partition and time is the wide-column pattern. Discord's primary key became ((channel_id, bucket), message_id): the partition key picks where a channel's messages for one time bucket live, and the message id, a Snowflake, sorts them inside. Key-value can't read a channel's range; one document per channel would grow forever; a graph is built for walks, not ranges.

recall.prompt: Nightwatch checks 200 sites every minute and saves every result as a row in one PostgreSQL table. After a year the 90-day uptime page, showing how often each site answered, takes 20 seconds, and the disk keeps growing. What would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Roll the results up ahead of time, per hour and per day, and have the uptime page read the rollups
A retention rule: delete raw results after a set age, once they're rolled up
Partition the raw table by time, or index it on (check, time), so a window reads only its own rows

recall.model: Uptime checks are time-series data, and the page reads 90 days of raw rows every time: 200 sites times 1,440 a day is 288,000 rows a day, about 25.9 million for 90 days. Roll them up ahead of time. A job counts each check's successes and attempts for every hour and day, and writes them into hourly and daily rollup tables. The uptime page reads those, a few thousand rows instead of millions. Add a retention rule that deletes raw results older than, say, 30 days once they're rolled up, which stops the disk growing. Partition the raw table by time, by day or month, so the retention job drops whole partitions and a recent window reads only its own; and index raw results on (check_id, checked_at) for the questions that still need them. TimescaleDB's hypertables and continuous aggregates do the same inside PostgreSQL. No new database needed.

recall.prompt: Mrs Rookwood's recursive owner-chain query has no cycle guard. It reaches the music box, whose 1991 sale leads back to the 1974 sale. What happens?
options: It stops after six steps, PostgreSQL's limit for recursion
PostgreSQL notices the repeated sale and stops by itself
It goes round the loop until something stops it
It skips the music box and goes on to the next object
recall.why: PostgreSQL's docs warn that the recursive part must eventually return no tuples, or else the query will loop indefinitely. There's no limit of six; that was the old query's six self-joins. UNION instead of UNION ALL only drops rows that repeat exactly, and a row that carries a depth or a path never does. The CYCLE clause, or a path column you check yourself, is what stops it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 8 months later. The chains run in 3.1 seconds and the chart in a quarter of one. In the summer a friend of Mrs Rookwood's built a provenance map, a picture of each object's owners, for the website on a graph store, and a job copies the sales into it from PostgreSQL every night at 02:00. At the autumn fair a woman bought a ship's clock at 11:00, and at 15:00 the map still showed the shop as its owner. On Sunday a sale was cancelled and deleted in PostgreSQL. The map still shows the buyer, and on Wednesday it still did.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What's going on, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The map is a copy refreshed once a night: new sales reach it the next morning, and the deleted sale was never removed because the job only adds
PostgreSQL stays the system of record: labels and anything that must be right read from it, and the map can be rebuilt from it
Copy each change, deletes included, as it happens, or drop the graph store and serve the map from the recursive query

coldCase.model: The map is a copy, and it's only as fresh as its last copy. The job runs at 02:00, so the clock sold at 11:00 reaches the map the next morning, and the job only adds and updates: a sale deleted in PostgreSQL is never removed from the graph store, so the buyer stays forever. That's data kept in two stores with no single transaction across them. PostgreSQL is the system of record: print labels from it, and treat the map as something you can rebuild from it at any time, and do rebuild it now. Then either copy each change as it happens, deletes included, with change data capture: read each change from PostgreSQL's log, its running list of changes, and apply it to the map, or ask whether the map needs a graph store at all, since the recursive query already walks every chain in 3.1 seconds and could serve it from one store.
